title: The Light Extracted from Hyle's Storehouses, Leaving Her a Dead Body
arc: At the appointed time the First Man was molded into the garment of flesh and sent into the war against Hyle, after which the Living Spirit's archons captured the elements of Darkness and built the cosmos as storehouses for the Greatness; once the living natures had been drawn out of those storehouses, what remained — Hyle herself — became inert matter, a body without a soul, the "Death of the Midst."
reading:
This teaching narrates the central operation of the cosmic war as a single movement: the descent of Divine Truth into the realm of self-love, the capture of darkness's elements, the construction of the cosmos as a system of storehouses, and the eventual hollowing-out of Hyle once her living natures have been extracted. The whole arc is governed by a single insight, given at the end through two carefully chosen analogies: when life is drawn out of a body, the body becomes incapable of any operation; in just this way, when the captive light is drawn out of Hyle, she is reduced to a dead corpse-substance.

The opening sets the appointed moment. At "the time when they sent forth" the molding of Man into the war, Divine Truth — the First Man — was clothed in the garment of nature, fashioned as a single garment to bear the conflict. This is the descent of the Divine Human into the natural for redemptive purposes: love and wisdom take on form precisely so that they can confront concupiscence on its own ground. Once clothed, "they ran at Matter, the Enthumesis" together with all her companion-falsities. The hunt has begun.

When something then "came up forth out of the Deep" — almost certainly the captured substance of darkness rising from the hells — the Living Spirit and his archons in turn ran after the elements that belonged to Darkness. From this seizure the operative Divine power "created from them this cosmos and the formations of all things, fashioned for the Greatness." This is the central correspondence of the teaching: the visible cosmos is not the Land of Darkness itself but a structure built out of captured darkness, a system of storehouses in which the elements are now held in service of the Father. The ordering Wisdom takes the very stuff of the enemy and refashions it as receptive form for divine good.

The teaching then shifts to a state of completion: the place of the storehouses of the elements has now been "emptied out" of all that was within it. The work of extraction has done what it set out to do; the living content has been drawn off, and what remains is the husk. To make this state intelligible, the master gives two natural likenesses.

The first is the lake. Lions run at the fish and birds in the water — at the natural truths submerged in receptive natural depth and at the thoughts that move in its medium of perception — while leaving behind "the middle and the others and the plants that grow within it." The predatory zeal seizes what is living and movable; the inert middle layer and the vegetation, which represent what cannot be quickened or borne up, are passed over. Just so, the storehouse of Death has had its living content seized: the counsels and dwellings of Hyle have been raided, the elements that could be redeemed have been carried off, and what is left is residue.

The second likeness is the body, and it carries the heart of the teaching. The body has great limbs joined to it, and these are sustained by small wellsprings — the inner channels of life that root all the limbs in one common origin. While a man is alive, these small wellsprings stand fast within him and supply every member; the limbs hold together because life flows through these inner roots. But when the soul departs from the body, no operation any longer exists in him; nothing stands fast; every member ceases its work. The soul is the one who works the operation; she is what makes the body do "every work" at all. Without her, the body is simply dead.

This likeness is then applied directly to Hyle. When she and all her powers existed in the abyss, her storehouses were themselves alive: their inner standing-fast was provided by the captive divine substance dwelling in them — the Living Soul held within her elements as their unwilling life-principle. Each falsity stood firm in its own storehouse only because something living was inhabiting it. But "at the time when their natures of nature were taken" — when the Five Sons of the First Man, the captive light dispersed through all her elements, were separated forth and drawn out — those storehouses with their elements became "inactive (argon)." No operation could come to be in them; they could do nothing. Hyle without the captive light is exactly what a body is without a soul: a corpse.

The teaching closes by naming this state precisely. Hyle is now "the Death of the Midst" — a dead body, a land without life, an existence without operation. This is the deep point of the whole arc. The cosmos is the place where Divine Truth has been crucified into matter so that, by its very dispersal through Hyle's storehouses, it can be drawn back out and Hyle herself emptied. The First Man's molding into the garment, the Living Spirit's seizure of the elements, the construction of the cosmic storehouses, and the eventual extraction of the living natures form one continuous operation. What looks like the building of the world is in fact the staging of an extraction; what looks like the Light's defeat in being clothed and crucified is the very mechanism by which Death is reduced to a soulless body.

Read this way, the teaching is a meditation on how the proprium is undone. Self-love seems alive only because it has captured something living from above; once the divine truth held within it is drawn back out through the redemptive economy, what remains of self-love is not a rival power but a corpse. The cosmos is the storehouse-system in which this draining happens, and its elements — fish, birds, limbs, wellsprings — are all images of the living content being pulled home.
